what_it_does: Non-volatile memory (NVM) is a type of storage that retains data even when power is cut — unlike ordinary RAM, which forgets everything when turned off. Programs that use NVM must explicitly issue flush instructions to push pending writes from volatile buffers into the permanent NVM; if a programmer misses or misorients a flush, a power failure can leave the data in a broken, inconsistent state (a crash-consistency bug). Existing tools to find these bugs work by running the program and testing specific scenarios, but they cannot guarantee correctness in all possible cases. This paper introduces a formal mathematical property called robustness for NVM crash consistency and proves that checking whether a corrupted post-crash memory state is possible reduces to a well-defined logical formula that an SMT solver (an automated theorem prover) can decide. A tool called PMVerify implements this approach, systematically exploring all possible partial executions and crash points without requiring the user to manually specify test scenarios.
